subject: math
domain: Number and Quantity — The Complex Number System
cluster: Use complex numbers in polynomial identities and equations
description: Students solve quadratic equations with real coefficients whose solutions are non-real complex numbers. They recognize from the discriminant $b^2-4ac<0$ that a quadratic has two complex-conjugate solutions, and they produce those solutions in standard form $a+bi$ using both completing the square (especially when $b=0$, e.g. $x^2+k=0$) and the quadratic formula. They simplify square roots of negative numbers using $\sqrt{-1}=i$ (so $\sqrt{-k}=i\sqrt{k}$ for $k>0$), reduce radicals, and write each solution as a conjugate pair $\frac{-b}{2a}\pm\frac{\sqrt{4ac-b^2}}{2a}\,i$. They also verify a complex solution by substitution and reconstruct a quadratic from a given complex-conjugate root pair.
subSkills: Compute the discriminant $b^2-4ac$ and classify the nature of the roots (two real, one repeated real, or two complex conjugates) by its sign
Simplify the square root of a negative number: rewrite $\sqrt{-k}$ as $i\sqrt{k}$ and reduce the radical (e.g. $\sqrt{-12}=2i\sqrt{3}$)
Solve a pure quadratic $x^2+k=0$ or $a x^2+c=0$ by isolating $x^2$ and taking the square root, yielding $\pm i\sqrt{k}$
Apply the quadratic formula $x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ when the discriminant is negative and simplify to standard form $a+bi$
Solve by completing the square and express the complex roots in $a+bi$ form
Write the two solutions as a complex-conjugate pair and present each in standard form with the real part and imaginary part identified
Verify that a complex number is a solution by substituting it back into the quadratic (using $i^2=-1$)
Reconstruct a quadratic (in factored or expanded form) from a given complex-conjugate root pair using sum and product of roots

problemArchetypes.name: Classify roots by the discriminant
problemArchetypes.example: Without solving, determine the nature of the roots of $2x^2-3x+5=0$. (Discriminant $=(-3)^2-4(2)(5)=9-40=-31<0$, so two complex-conjugate solutions.)

problemArchetypes.name: Quadratic formula leaving a reduced radical in the imaginary part
problemArchetypes.example: Solve $x^2+2x+5=0$ — wait, that reduces cleanly; instead $x^2-2x+4=0$. ($x=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}{2}=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{-12}}{2}=\dfrac{2\pm2i\sqrt{3}}{2}=1\pm i\sqrt{3}$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Solve by completing the square
problemArchetypes.example: Solve $x^2+6x+34=0$ by completing the square. ($(x+3)^2=-25$, so $x+3=\pm5i$, giving $x=-3\pm5i$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Verify a complex solution by substitution
Reconstruct a quadratic from a complex-conjugate root pair
problemArchetypes.example: Find a quadratic with real coefficients having $3-2i$ as a root. (Conjugate $3+2i$ is also a root; sum $=6$, product $=9+4=13$, so $x^2-6x+13=0$.)

Easy.description: One- or two-step problems with $b=0$ or a direct discriminant check. The student isolates $x^2$ in a pure quadratic and takes a square root that lands on a clean pure-imaginary value $\pm ni$, or classifies roots from a single discriminant computation. No quadratic formula with a nonzero linear term, no radical to reduce.
constraints: Equation is $x^2+k=0$ or $ax^2+c=0$ with $k$ a perfect square after dividing out $a$, so roots are $\pm ni$ with $n$ an integer
OR a single discriminant computation that asks only to classify the roots (real vs. complex), not to solve
Imaginary part is an integer; no reduced radical and no real part
Numbers stay small (coefficients with absolute value $\le 50$)

Medium.description: Full quadratic formula or completing the square on $x^2+bx+c=0$ (or $a=1$) with a negative discriminant that produces a clean conjugate pair $p\pm qi$ where the radical simplifies to an integer. Both a real part and an integer imaginary part are present. This is the central band where a typical solve lives.
constraints: Leading coefficient $a=1$ (or divides out cleanly) and $b\neq0$
Discriminant is the negative of a perfect square so $\sqrt{4ac-b^2}$ is an integer
Solutions take the form $p\pm qi$ with integer $p$ and $q$
May require solving by completing the square as the named method

Hard.description: Multi-step problems where the imaginary part is a reduced radical and/or the leading coefficient $a\neq1$ produces fractional real and imaginary parts, plus the inverse and verification tasks. Includes reconstructing a quadratic from a complex root, verifying a root by substitution with $i^2=-1$, or simplifying $\sqrt{-k}$ where $k$ is not a perfect square.
constraints: $\sqrt{4ac-b^2}$ is NOT a perfect square, so the imaginary part is a reduced radical such as $i\sqrt{3}$ or $\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2}i$
OR leading coefficient $a\neq1$ yielding fractional real and/or imaginary parts (e.g. $\dfrac{1}{2}\pm\dfrac{1}{2}i$)
OR reconstruct the quadratic from a single given complex-conjugate root using sum and product of roots
OR verify a given complex solution by full substitution, correctly applying $i^2=-1$
Exact values required (radicals and fractions), never rounded decimals

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Treats $\sqrt{-k}$ as a real number or as $-\sqrt{k}$, dropping the imaginary unit
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $x^2+25=0$ writes $x=\pm5$ (or $x=-5$) instead of $x=\pm5i$, ignoring that the root is non-real

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Splits a negative radical incorrectly: $\sqrt{-a}\cdot\sqrt{-b}=\sqrt{ab}$ as if both were real
Sign error on $i^2$: uses $i^2=1$ instead of $i^2=-1$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: When verifying, evaluates $(2+3i)^2=4+12i+9$ (treating $9i^2$ as $+9$) and concludes the substitution fails or yields the wrong sum

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Misuses the discriminant sign, reading $b^2-4ac<0$ as 'no solutions' rather than 'two complex solutions'
commonMisconceptions.distractor: States $x^2-4x+13=0$ has no solution because the discriminant is negative, instead of giving $2\pm3i$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets to divide the entire numerator (both real and imaginary parts) by $2a$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $x^2-4x+13=0$ writes $x=4\pm3i$ (dividing only one term) instead of $x=2\pm3i$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Drops or mis-signs the linear coefficient in $-b$ when applying the quadratic formula
Fails to reduce the radical in the imaginary part
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $x^2-2x+4=0$ leaves $x=1\pm i\sqrt{12}$ or $\dfrac{2\pm i\sqrt{12}}{2}$ instead of simplifying $\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt{3}$ to get $1\pm i\sqrt{3}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: When reconstructing from a complex root, uses only the given root and forgets its conjugate (or sign-errors the product)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Given root $3-2i$, writes $x-(3-2i)=0$ (a non-real-coefficient linear factor) or computes the product of roots as $9-4=5$ instead of $9+4=13$, giving $x^2-6x+5$
